name: Calendars and tasks
summary: How to turn a to-do list into a day you can actually do, agree on shared plans, and not lose a task after a reschedule or a missed reminder.
lead:
In the morning there are ten things on the list and two free hours between meetings. Then the appointment time changes, the child has to be picked up earlier, and the reminder arrives when it is already too late to leave. A good planner helps rebuild the day: see what is still possible and what will have to move.

Quick capture frees your memory only on condition that you can get back to what you captured. That is why ease of entry, schedule changes you can follow and the survival of agreements are linked in this category. What follows looks at how they work in personal errands, in a family and in a working day.

audiencesArt.alt: Different jobs in the “Calendars and tasks” category.

audiences.title: Write the thought down and don’t lose it
audiences.body: A person wants to write a thought down quickly and stop holding it in memory. What they need is a familiar place to enter it, a visible save and an easy second look. Extra parameters are useful later, if they really do help get the thing done.

audiences.title: Build a day you can actually do
audiences.body: A person lines meetings up against tasks and rebuilds the day when things change. What matters is seeing the time available and the nearest action that can be done. A large job may need breaking down, and a meeting that has moved may need the order reconsidered.

audiences.title: Fit work and family plans together
audiences.body: A family combines different people’s activities, work and irregular shifts. What is needed is a shared view where the members and the kinds of commitment can be told apart. When something changes, it matters to know whether one day is affected or a repeating schedule.

sections.title: Assemble a day that can actually be done
sections.intro: First a person needs to save the intention. Then to compare it with the time available. These happen at different moments: at night a short note is enough, by morning a choice between several things is already needed.

observations.title: Capture now, sort it out later
passages: For a short thought what matters is how reachable the entry point is. The author prefers a permanent add bar to a separate button: it puts fewer actions between the intention and the record. Having to pick a project or a date at that moment can only hold things up.

Trust comes later, when the record can actually be found. Another user has spent years dropping any thought in here, at night included, and no longer holds them in memory. Speed is useful together with a predictable way back to what was written down.

A simple list has a value of its own as well. The author of the next review praises a tool that helps him compose, order and complete tasks without extra noise. That experience does not confirm the need for a complicated system of projects.

A new record may not have a due date yet. “Ask about the certificate” does not yet mean “do it today”. A place for unsorted thoughts lets you keep them and leave assigning a time until you plan the day. For those who like writing by hand, a digital page linked to the calendar can do the same job.

quotes.text: It's a great app but I need couple of changes: Please put the 'Add New Task' Bar back. The '+' circle to add a new task is ok but the Bar all the way on top is soooooo much faster and easier.

I've been using Todoist for at least seven years now and I have it well integrated into my daily life. It is the one place I can throw anything at any time and not have to think about it again. Wake up at 3am with a thought, add it and I know I won't lose it.

The Minimalist app stands out by doing the opposite of most productivity tools — it removes all the noise. The interface is clean, intuitive, and beautifully simple, focusing purely on helping you list, organize, and complete your tasks.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Capture now, sort it out later”.

placements.title: Capture now, sort it out later

observations.title: See what really fits into the day
passages: Meetings take up specific time and determine what is left for tasks. Two independent lists do not always help you notice an overfilled day. On a shared timeline the link is visible: a new call shortens the interval in which the person meant to finish something.

Another author keeps the app precisely because the calendar and the tasks are in the same place. That confirms the convenience of a shared place, but does not yet prove the value of automatic scheduling: being able to line the records up yourself may be enough.

A request to rearrange things with the time recalculated is more specific. The author wants to change the order of actions and see the new boundaries. What matters here is the preview: which tasks will move and what will stop fitting. Changes to meetings that have been agreed must not be hidden behind an automatic rearrangement.

For field work the free interval also depends on the drive. For a pro in a salon it depends on the length of the service and on setting the place up. These are separate ways of developing the general principle, not a reason to add routes and client booking to every personal planner.

quotes.text: I like seeing my calendar and tasks in one screen. The time-sensitive information on my calendar affects what tasks I can get done and when.
I like how you have both the calendar and tasks on the same app it makes it useful and is the reason why I kept it after downloading so many other apps that are similar.

This is a great concept, and I haven't found another app like it. But it's lacking some things that would make it better. It would be nice if you could drag and drop items to a different order and have the start and stop times automatically adjust.

placements.title: See what really fits into the day
Prepare for a work visit
placements.body: A client booking links the time of the service with the preparation: the photos and the client’s wishes have to reach the pro before the appointment.

observations.title: Work out where to start
passages: For one person starting work means first seeing every assignment in one place. A student values the app gathering different lists and shopping together without the order falling apart. A scenario like that calls for an overview you can read, not for every item to be broken down.

With household cleaning the difficulty is different: it is not clear where to start or how much counts as manageable. The next author values actions that have been laid out in advance. Here the product helps pick the nearest step instead of reading a long, undefined list.

Another user is helped by the structure of work sessions, with which he carries projects on for several months. No universal concentration technique can be picked out of this. But the difference between the jobs is visible: gathering commitments, reducing the scale of an action, or staying with the work you have chosen.

That is why a visual timeline and a semester planner should not come out of the same set of settings. In the first case what is tested is returning to the current action after a distraction; in the second, the link between assignments, courses, due dates and the real load of the week.

quotes.text: As a college student with severe ADHD this is the perfect user friendly app to keep all my different to do and shopping lists organized and in one place.

TLDR: had helped me breakdown cleaning in a way i can actually manage on a regular basis. I hate cleaning to death and whenever i want to do it, I feel so overwhelmed about where to start. Sweepy always knows what needs to be done.

This is the best app I have found (after trying so many) for managing focus and procrastination. After 4 months I'm still going strong in my work and finishing projects which would've been impossible to achieve without the structure that this brings.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Work out where to start”.

sections.title: Rebuild the plan when life has changed
sections.intro: A personal list gradually meets the family’s schedule, shifts, repeating chores and notifications. Now every edit can affect another person or next week.

observations.title: Separate who is busy from who has agreed
passages: A large family combines the events of several people. One calendar helps you see the shared day, but on its own it does not explain whose each activity is. In the next review that is the main situation of use.

A member’s color cuts the time it takes to read: one look is enough to see whose event is coming up. Here the styling carries a specific meaning. It is especially useful when the same activities repeat for different children.

With several jobs another distinction is added — shifts, days off and personal plans. A nurse describes using the schedule for two jobs and for her grandchildren’s errands. A shared view has to preserve these distinctions rather than turn everything into the same kind of busy.

And there is a further question: who is not merely taking part but responsible for the action? “Practice at six” does not say who will pick the child up. Assigning someone responsible and confirming a reschedule is a possible development of the family scenario. For helping someone close, a list like this covers agreements about visits and household errands; it does not replace what specialists prescribe.

quotes.text: I have a big family with five kids ranging from baby to preteen. My older kids are active in multiple sports. My husband and I also have different activities we do. This is the best calendar app I've ever used.

If you have a big family and like to know what direction everyone is going, this is the app for you, especially if you have several active teenagers like myself. Each member of the home has a color, so just a quick glance at the calendar.

I am a nurse who works here and there in a clinic through the week and just picked up a local travel job. This keeps me in line with both jobs and activities my grand babies have going on. I've used another app for a while but kept noticing it wasn't cutting it.

placements.title: Separate who is busy from who has agreed

observations.title: Move it once and keep the whole schedule
passages: A repeat consists of a rule and individual occurrences. Skipping today’s task does not mean giving it up for good; changing one shift does not mean rebuilding the whole schedule. If the app mixes these actions up, the person has to restore the sequence or clear out the duplicates that appeared.

Before a change, its scope has to be shown clearly: this occurrence only, or future repeats. Afterwards, the next occurrence. A check like that makes the behavior clear straight away, while the person still remembers the intention, rather than several days later when a task turns out to be missing.

A repeat can also rest on a different basis: every two weeks on Mondays, or two weeks after it was done. After a skip those rules give different dates. Better to offer a clear example of when the task will next appear, right there in the setup. Then the person sees the behavior before trusting it with a payment, servicing equipment or a specialist appointment.

quotes.text: I tried two competing programs before this one, and neither could successfully do recurring tasks the way I needed them to. This program accomplishes this mostly without incident; occasionally a task appears in Google calendar twice.

When I delete a task for the day, which is set to be a daily recurring task, it doesn't keep that setting continuously, so I have to hunt for it in the deleted tasks section, or enter it again. Then I end up with a huge amount of the same task.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Move it once and keep the whole schedule”.

observations.title: Remind in a way that makes the action clear
passages: An ordinary alert is easily lost among the other notifications. The author of the next review values being able to hear the wording of the needed action straight away. A voice restores the meaning of the reminder rather than just making it louder.

Another person describes the exact cause: he notices the vibration but no longer remembers what it referred to. So the name of the task and a clear action after the alert matter more than the choice of a new sound.

Expressiveness does not help, though, if the alert never arrives at all. One author entered birthdays and never once got a notification. Setup should end with a test alert on the device, so the person notices the problem before the date that matters.

It is useful to separate the time of the event from the time to get ready: “appointment at three” and “time to leave” help at different moments. After a snooze the new alert time should be visible. These are testable actions that can be improved without promising flawless delivery of every reminder.

quotes.text: I have so many notifications on my phone that I end up tuning them all out. That's bad when you forget almost everything without something reminding you. This allows me to yell at myself from my own phone about what specifically I need to do.

With ADHD, I have trouble with working memory so, even with a calendar reminder, I forget what I'm doing and don't get out the door on time. Often times I set my watch to buzz or my phone to chime but I don't remember what the buzz or chime was for.

I spent a lot of time entering birthday's and not once have I ever been alerted. If it's something I'm doing wrong, then this app is designed poorly or the set up is not very clear on the instructions.

placements.title: Remind in a way that makes the action clear

sections.title: Keep trusting your own calendar
sections.intro: Over time the planner becomes the place where other people’s agreements, work deadlines and important dates are kept. Reliability here shows in the ordinary continuation: open the list you know and find exactly what you left in it.

observations.title: Don’t mistake loading for lost records
passages: An empty list can mean different things: the record was not saved, the phone has not received the data yet, or the app did not open properly. From the outside, for the user, it is one and the same loss of the plan. With no explanation they have to hunt for tasks on other devices and work out where the correct version ended up.

Show the state of saving and updating separately from the contents of the list, and leave a path to recovery. When choosing a planner it is worth testing one record on the devices you use, and your access to your own history. Reliable continuation supports the main work with tasks; it is not a separate reason to complicate the product.

Uncertainty is especially painful: delete the empty project, wait, or enter the tasks again? While the state is unknown, it is safer to keep the last available copy and show when it was updated. When two devices conflict, it helps to let the person compare the changes. Successful sync means not only the record appearing on the second screen but also being able to understand what happened to the edits.

quotes.text: The whole point of this is to keep track of saved dates so you won't miss anything. Today I opened up the app and it deleted ALL OF MY EVENTS.

Loved until app deleted all alarms & won't restore. I guess the developer gave up on listening to me. I haven't gotten another response & I am very disappointed that he does not care that the app doesn't work.

I have used this for a couple years and it seemed to work well. But recently when reviewing all tasks and updating multiple projects, I realized tasks were missing on the iOS phone app. After much concern and debugging (project showed empty on phone but had tasks on web app).

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Don’t mistake loading for lost records”.

observations.title: Carry on working as usual after an update
passages: A planner you are used to is valuable for the way of working you know. The first author spent several years creating classes and tasks without having to learn anything complicated. His account shows that an update has to take into account the path already mastered, even if the styling looks dated.

Another user describes the former set of free capabilities: work sessions, time tracking and blocking distractions. The excerpt does not make clear what exactly changed after the update. But it is clear which way of working he needed; changes are worth explaining through that accustomed scenario.

The third review is about price: an annual subscriber says the cost went up without notice. That is a separate part of trust. The renewal terms and access to earlier records should be clear before the change, whatever the new styling.

For a product already in use, testing the accustomed path is valuable: write a task down, move a meeting, find something completed. It will show the cost of a change for someone who has already trusted the app with their plans. For a new product the same observations help pick a durable scenario, but they do not prove demand for one more universal calendar.

quotes.text: I've used this app for four years at this point, and I used to really love the app. The interface wasn't overly complicated, and it was easy to create classes and tasks. While the design wasn't overly modernized and sleek like most scheduling apps now, it worked.

Prior to the latest update I absolutely loved the app. I was a free user, and even then it did exactly what I wanted it to: set pomodoro sessions, track my time among different tasks — it was perfect. The option to block apps was there.
I got this app a good while ago and ended up getting the yearly subscription for all the features. Fast forward to now and they've increased the subscription without notifying current subscribers.

conclusion.title: Rebuild the day without losing the agreements
conclusion.body:
The strong scenario for this category is changing a day that has already been put together. A new meeting, a longer task, a swapped shift: the person has to see the consequences and decide what to move. Adding new kinds of list will not help if a change like that loses records or affects the whole schedule without explanation.

For a new product it is worth picking one setting: study, family agreements or work visits. Each has its own time limits and its own responsible people. For a calendar already in use, predictable editing and reminders you can understand matter more. Testing on a full day will show more than setting up a beautiful empty schedule: will the person be able to carry on with their tasks after a change, without starting a second calendar?
